title: Semilinear action on a finite normalization model
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $S$ be an integral projective finite-type $k$-scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme, def-kun-projective, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], put $K=k(S)$ [def-sc-function-field], and let $M/K$ be a finite field extension [def-pc-field-extension]. Let $J$ be a finite group acting on $S$ and on $k$ compatibly with the structure map, write $h_j$ for its action on $S$, and suppose $\sigma:J\to\operatorname{Aut}(M)$ is a group homomorphism with
$$\sigma_j|_K=(h_{j^{-1}})^*:K\longrightarrow K.$$
Here $h^*$ is pullback on the generic stalk, and group actions are allowed to be nonfaithful and to move $k$. Let $u:B\to S$ be the normalization of $S$ in $M$ [def-fin-normalization-extension]. Then $B$ is normal integral and projective of finite type over $k$, $u$ is finite and surjective [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-weil-surjective-morphism], and the canonical map $\eta_B:\operatorname{Spec}M\to B$ identifies the generic point and function field of $B$ with $M$. The generic fibre $B\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K$ is $\operatorname{Spec}M$. There is a unique action $a:J\to\operatorname{Aut}(B)$ satisfying
$$u\circ a_j=h_j\circ u,\qquad a_j\circ\eta_B=\eta_B\circ\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma_j^{-1}).$$
This action on $B$ is compatible with the specified action on $k$. Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. Projective means admitting a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the target, with no linearization of the group action assumed. The generic fibre is the fibre product of [def-pc-fibre-product].

proof.text: Write $p:S\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $f:\operatorname{Spec}M\to\operatorname{Spec}K\to S$. Projectivity makes $p$ proper, hence separated. Since $p$ is of finite type over an affine scheme, $S$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Apply the normalization-in-a-residue-field-extension theorem at the generic point of $S$, whose residue field is $K$. Its specified relative normalization is exactly $B$, and its generic morphism is $\eta_B$. Thus $B$ is normal integral, $u$ is integral, $u\eta_B=f$, and $\eta_B$ identifies its function field with $M$. The same theorem supplies the qcqs hypothesis on $f$ needed below.

source.place: Tags 035H definition-normalization-X-in-Y, 035I lemma-characterize-normalization and 035L lemma-normal-normalization; apply at the generic point.

proof.text: Apply finiteness of normalization in a finite function-field extension to the integral finite-type $k$-scheme $S$ and $M/K$: $u$ is finite. A finite morphism is closed. Its image contains the generic point of $S$, since $u\eta_B=f$, so its closed image is all of the integral scheme $S$. Thus $u$ is surjective.

Use the finite-over-projective theorem with base $\operatorname{Spec}k$, $T=S$, $Y=B$; $p$ is projective in its convention, since it has a closed immersion into some $\mathbf P^N_k$ over $k$ and is quasi-compact, being of finite type. A field is Noetherian because its only ideals are $0$ and $k$. This base is affine, so the theorem gives a closed immersion $B\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_k$ for some finite $N$, exactly the required convention. Also $u$ is proper because it is finite, hence of finite type by the definition of proper; composition with $p$ shows $B$ is of finite type over $k$.

source.place: Tag 0GK4 lemma-normalize-projective, proof using finite projectivity and composition; global embedding over the affine field base follows the cited finite-over-projective statement.

proof.text: Choose a nonempty affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $S$ and write $C=\overline A^{\,M}$. The affine normalization description gives $u^{-1}U=\operatorname{Spec}C$, with its structure map induced by $A\subset C\subset M$. Put $T=A\setminus\{0\}$; $T^{-1}A=K$. Integral-closure localization identifies $T^{-1}C$ with the integral closure of $K$ in $T^{-1}M=M$. Every $z\in M$ is integral over $K$: linear dependence of $1,z,\ldots,z^{[M:K]}$, divided by its last nonzero coefficient, gives a monic relation. Thus $T^{-1}C=M$. The tensor-localization isomorphism $C\otimes_AK\cong T^{-1}C$ sends $c\otimes(a/s)$ to $ac/s$; its inverse sends $c/s$ to $c\otimes(1/s)$, well-defined by the localization relations. Since $f$ and $\operatorname{Spec}K\to S$ factor through the open $U$ and $u^{-1}U=B\times_SU$, one has $B\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K=u^{-1}U\times_U\operatorname{Spec}K$. The affine fibre-product theorem, with $R=A$, now gives $B\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K=\operatorname{Spec}M$, canonically with the map $\eta_B$.

source.place: Tag 035H definition-normalization-X-in-Y, affine charts; algebra.tex Tag 0307 lemma-integral-closure-localize; schemes.tex Tag 01I4 lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes.

proof.text: For $j\in J$ put $t_j=\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma_j^{-1})$. Since pullback reverses composition, the hypothesis gives $(h_j)^*|_K=\sigma_j^{-1}|_K$, hence $f\circ t_j=h_j\circ f$. The map $q_j=h_j^{-1}\circ u:B\to S$ is integral: postcomposing an integral morphism with a scheme isomorphism merely relabels the affine charts in its definition. There is a factorization $f=q_j\circ(\eta_B\circ t_j)$. Apply the relative-normalization universal property to $f$, $q_j$, and $\eta_B\circ t_j$ to obtain $a_j:B\to B$ with $q_j a_j=u$ and $a_j\eta_B=\eta_Bt_j$. Multiplying the first equation by $h_j$ gives $u a_j=h_j u$. The uniqueness clause applies too, since integral implies affine; it says that any two maps with these two equations agree.

source.place: Tag 035I lemma-characterize-normalization, applied to the integral factorization with target map h_j^{-1} composed with u.

proof.text: The identity of $B$ satisfies the two equations for $j=1$, so uniqueness gives $a_1=1$. For $i,j\in J$, $u a_i a_j=h_i h_j u=h_{ij}u$. Moreover $t_i\circ t_j=\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma_j^{-1}\circ\sigma_i^{-1})=\operatorname{Spec}(\sigma_{ij}^{-1})=t_{ij}$, so $a_i a_j\eta_B=\eta_Bt_{ij}$. Uniqueness for the integral target map $h_{ij}^{-1}u$ gives $a_i a_j=a_{ij}$. Taking $i=j^{-1}$ on both sides makes $a_{j^{-1}}$ the two-sided inverse of $a_j$. Therefore these maps form the asserted action by automorphisms, even if either original action has a kernel.

source.place: Tag 035I lemma-characterize-normalization, uniqueness; elementary multiplication of the defining commuting squares.

proof.text: Any other asserted action has, for each $j$, the two equations characterizing $a_j$, so the same uniqueness proves equality of the actions. If $b_j$ is the specified geometric action on $\operatorname{Spec}k$, compatibility on $S$ means $p h_j=b_j p$. Therefore $(pu)a_j=p h_j u=b_j(pu)$. This proves compatibility with the given action on $k$ without any requirement that the action fix $k$ or linearize a projective embedding.

source.place: Tag 035I lemma-characterize-normalization, uniqueness, followed by composition with the structure morphism.
